newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: S.Lanka rebel attacks send ripple through Jaffna.
newsitem.headline: S.Lanka rebel attacks send ripple through Jaffna.

text.p: A series of attacks by Tamil Tiger rebels on civilian ships in Sri Lanka's north reflects an attempt to undermine government claims that life is returning to normal in the war-ravaged Jaffna region, analysts and officials said on Wednesday.
"It is obvious. The people in Jaffna are finally leading a normal life and naturally, (the rebels) would not like that," military spokesman Brigadier Sarath Munasinghe told Reuters.
Government forces took control of the Jaffna peninsula in April last year after a lengthy offensive during which most of the population fled to the Wanni mainland further south.
The government has since given wide publicity to life returning to normal in the peninsula, which was under rebel control for nearly a decade.
The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in Sri Lanka's north and east, appear bent on crippling that campaign, analysts said.
Diplomats said the rebels were also trying to scare foreign shipping companies, which have leased their vessels to the government to carry refugees from the Wanni to Jaffna.
Tiger rebels seized a North Korean merchant ship late on Monday some eight km (five miles) off Point Pedro on Jaffna, about 320 km (200 miles) north of the capital Colombo.
The LTTE's clandestine Voice of Tigers radio said one of the Morang Bong's 38 North Korean crew members was killed during a shoot-out while the rebels took control of the ship.
Last week, they set fire to a refugee ship off the northwestern coast and took away its nine crew, including two Indonesians who were later freed.
The ships were being used to ferry food and refugees between Jaffna and the rest of Sri Lanka. Only the crew were on board when they were attacked.
Food and other essential supplies are taken to Jaffna by air or sea as there is no land route connecting the peninsula with the rest of the island.

Some 20,000 Sri Lankan troops are battling the Tiger rebels to open a highway through the rebel-held Wanni region toward Jaffna. But the offensive launched in May has been slowed by fierce rebel resistance.
Encouraged by news that life was returning to normal in Jaffna, tens of thousands of people have returned to their homes since the beginning of this year, military and government officials say.
"Foreign ships have been chartered because local shippers have refused to ferry food and people to Jaffna. The LTTE is obviously trying to scare them now," an Asian diplomat said.
Following the two incidents, at least five other ships hired by the government to ferry people and supplies to Jaffna have halted operations, the Island newspaper reported on Wednesday.
The Asian diplomat also said that the Sri Lankan navy, which had stopped escorting supply ships in the north, has recently fought the LTTE's "Sea Tigers" naval wing, sinking several rebel boats.

"It's possible the LTTE want the heat off their naval wing. By targeting civilian ships they are forcing the Sri Lankan navy to escort them again. If the navy starts escorting these ships, its force will be divided and they may not be able to hit LTTE boats in the same way as they are doing now," he said.
